column4: The section’s root gloss ر ف ع includes raising a building and pairs it with raised remembrance; this verse joins both: houses are permitted “أَن تُرْفَعَ وَيُذْكَرَ فِيهَا اسْمُهُ,” making construction and remembrance one scene.

The section’s root gloss وَضْع is setting something down; this verse says the Messenger “يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ” (removes their burden) and their shackles, directly pairing the image of a load put aside with release from burdens.

The section’s root ر ف ع is explicitly used of raising a structure; this verse has Abraham and Ishmael raise the House’s foundations (“يَرْفَعُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ الْقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ”) while asking their Lord to accept their work.

The section contrasts the House’s being placed with its foundations being raised; this verse says the first House for people was “وُضِعَ لِلنَّاسِ” at Bakkah, giving the same sanctuary the placed state paired with 2:127.

The section’s dictionary form نَقَضَ covers undoing a firmly made rope; this verse stages a woman unraveling her spun yarn after it was strong (“نَقَضَتْ غَزْلَهَا مِن بَعْدِ قُوَّةٍ”), the section’s clearest counter-image to the back under strain.

The section cites oath-breaking as a form of undoing; this preceding verse explicitly forbids breaking oaths after making them firm (“وَلَا تَنقُضُوا الْأَيْمَانَ بَعْدَ تَوْكِيدِهَا”). The next ayah, 16:92, supplies the yarn image; this row states the oath’s own contribution.

The section names the dictionary extension from undoing a built tie to breaking a covenant; this verse describes people who “يَنقُضُونَ عَهْدَ اللَّهِ مِن بَعْدِ مِيثَاقِهِ,” matching that extension directly.

The section’s dictionary form الْعُقْدَة is a knot and it distinguishes a knot loosened for rescue from yarn destructively unraveled; Moses asks, “وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِي,” a direct speech-knot release.

Moses’s “رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي” directly repeats the section’s chest-opening image. The linked 20:27 adds the request to untie his tongue’s knot; this ayah contributes the chest-opening side of that paired prayer.

The section names root ص د ر through the chest in 94:1; here guidance opens the chest toward Islam while misguidance makes it narrow and constricted, a specific opening/boundary that clarifies the bodily image.

The section’s root ر ف ع means lifting a set object and also raising a building; this verse applies the same action to the heavens, “رَفَعَ السَّمَاوَاتِ بِغَيْرِ عَمَدٍ تَرَوْنَهَا,” shifting the lift from body and remembrance to cosmic structure.
The section cites this verse for the building sense of root ر ف ع: the sky’s height is raised and proportioned (“رَفَعَ سَمْكَهَا فَسَوَّاهَا”), a direct architectural counterpart to the lifted name.

The section explicitly reads this verse’s two verbs together: the sky is raised and the balance placed (“رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ الْمِيزَانَ”), joining its paired acts of lifting and setting down in a single creation scene.
The section identifies this as the next placed object after the raised sky and placed balance: “وَالْأَرْضَ وَضَعَهَا لِلْأَنَامِ” sets the earth for living beings.

The section explicitly treats the camel, sky, mountains, and earth as one scene. This ayah opens it by asking how the camel was created; 88:18–20 then carry the gaze to raised sky, erected mountains, and spread earth.
This ayah asks how the sky was raised (“كَيْفَ رُفِعَتْ”), the same physical elevation developed in the section; 88:19 and 88:20 complete its linked mountain-and-earth scene.
This is the section’s explicit example of root ن ص ب applied to mountains: “كَيْفَ نُصِبَتْ,” set up as projecting objects, extending the image from the upright stake to a landscape.
The section names this as the earth’s counterpart after raised sky and erected mountains; the ayah asks how the earth was spread (“كَيْفَ سُطِحَتْ”), completing that vertical-to-ground scene.

The section’s dictionary form نَقَضَ includes dismantling a solidly built structure; here a building is attacked from its foundations and its roof falls on its people, a concrete collapse that gives the section’s cracking-structure image an external counterpart.

The section treats a sound build undone as an image of collapse; this verse contrasts a foundation on devotion with a building on an eroding bank that collapses with its builder (“فَانْهَارَ بِهِ”), making the stability boundary explicit.
The section’s load is removed from the back; this verse depicts people carrying their burdens “عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ,” the same body-and-load scene under the opposite condition.

The section’s dictionary form الْعَقْد names a knot and its extension to covenants; this verse speaks of “عَقَّدتُّمُ الْأَيْمَانَ,” bound oaths, putting the section’s knot-and-oath link into a specific Quranic formulation.
The section’s dictionary form الْعَقْد is a knot that can be undone; this verse uses the matching form “عُقْدَةَ النِّكَاحِ” for the marriage tie and sets a boundary on when it may be contracted.

The section’s yarn and covenant images turn on a bond being undone; this verse’s rope of God is to be held together (“وَاعْتَصِمُوا بِحَبْلِ اللَّهِ جَمِيعًا وَلَا تَفَرَّقُوا”), a specific image of binding cohesion against unraveling.
The section develops hardship alongside promised ease; this verse gives God’s promise “سَيَجْعَلُ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا,” the same specific transition from hardship to ease.

The section says remembrance is raised; here good speech ascends to God and righteous action raises it (“الْكَلِمُ الطَّيِّبُ يَصْعَدُ إِلَيْهِ وَالْعَمَلُ الصَّالِحُ يَرْفَعُهُ”), a close parallel for elevated mention through words.

The section depicts a load pressing on a back and then being removed; this prayer asks God not to make the community carry a burden (“وَلَا تُحَمِّلْنَا إِصْرًا”), a specific appeal at the imposition side of that bodily image.

The section develops sky and earth as a structure scene; this verse calls the sky a “بِنَاءً” above an earth made a resting spread (“فِرَاشًا”), giving that architectural pairing a related formulation.

This verse joins heavens made without visible pillars to mountains cast into the earth; it repeats the section’s two specific creation images of supported sky and set mountains, even though it uses different verbs.
The section treats the sky as a structure whose height is raised; this verse says, “وَالسَّمَاءَ بَنَيْنَاهَا بِأَيْدٍ,” making the construction itself explicit.
The section’s 88:19–20 scene links erected mountains with the earth; this verse likewise joins earth spread out and mountains cast into it (“وَالْأَرْضَ مَدَدْنَاهَا وَأَلْقَيْنَا فِيهَا رَوَاسِيَ”).
This repeated earth-and-mountains scene also says the earth is spread and firm mountains cast into it, directly corresponding to the landscape sequence the section develops.
The section describes earth as placed for living beings; this verse calls it a cradle made for its addressees (“جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الْأَرْضَ مَهْدًا”), specifying the earth’s supporting role.
This verse pairs earth made a settled place with sky as a structure (“الْأَرْضَ قَرَارًا وَالسَّمَاءَ بِنَاءً”), a direct variant of the section’s earth-and-raised-sky construction scene.

The section’s House passage pairs its placement for people with raised foundations; this verse identifies the House’s assigned place for Abraham (“بَوَّأْنَا لِإِبْرَاهِيمَ مَكَانَ الْبَيْتِ”), adding the site to that same sanctuary scene.

The section treats the sky as raised construction; this verse says seven strong structures were built above the addressees (“وَبَنَيْنَا فَوْقَكُمْ سَبْعًا شِدَادًا”), a specific parallel in the same sky-building image.

The section’s dictionary entry for root ع س ر gives a peg game in which an upright piece is knocked out; this verse calls mountains “أَوْتَادًا” (pegs), a related fixed-upright image whose function is the reverse: anchoring rather than removal.
The section’s landscape sequence includes mountains erected; this verse says the mountains were firmly set (“وَالْجِبَالَ أَرْسَاهَا”), a related account of their placement in the earth.
In the linked 20:27 prayer, Moses asks that a knot be untied from his tongue; this next ayah states the release’s purpose, that people understand his speech (“يَفْقَهُوا قَوْلِي”).

Moses says his chest constricts and his tongue does not flow (“وَيَضِيقُ صَدْرِي وَلَا يَنطَلِقُ لِسَانِي”); this gives a concrete blocked state against the section’s chest-opening and the knot-loosening prayer in 20:27.
The section names root ص د ر through an opened chest; this verse describes a chest opened to Islam and contrasts it with hard hearts, giving the image a spiritual opening and its boundary.

The section’s root ع س ر is paired with ease; this verse makes that transition concrete for a debtor, “ذُو عُسْرَةٍ” receiving respite until “مَيْسَرَةٍ,” a particular burden eased in its own context.

The section develops the hardship/ease pairing; this verse states that God wants ease and not hardship (“يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ بِكُمُ الْيُسْرَ وَلَا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ الْعُسْرَ”), making the opposition explicit.

The section’s dictionary form الْعَقْد is a knot and its extension to a bond; this verse names “عُقْدَةُ النِّكَاحِ” in a divorce settlement, showing the marriage tie as a held bond in the very setting where it may be released.
This verse names the breaking of a firm covenant (“نَقْضِهِم مِّيثَاقَهُمْ”), another direct use of the section’s root extension from undoing a built tie to breaking a pledge.

The section connects dismantling a tie with breach of covenant; this verse describes people who break their covenant repeatedly (“يَنقُضُونَ عَهْدَهُمْ فِي كُلِّ مَرَّةٍ”), adding repetition to the same act.
The section’s root extension is covenant-breaking; this verse describes the opposite boundary, people who fulfill God’s covenant and “لَا يَنقُضُونَ الْمِيثَاقَ.”
This verse repeats the section’s direct covenant-breaking image and adds cutting what God commanded to be joined; that severed bond makes the undoing concrete beyond the covenant itself.

The section’s oath and covenant examples describe a pledge being broken; here opponents break their oaths after their covenant (“نَّكَثُوا أَيْمَانَهُم مِّن بَعْدِ عَهْدِهِمْ”), the same breach in a distinct treaty context.
The section’s root ر ف ع includes physically lifting an object; this verse says Idris was raised to a high place (“وَرَفَعْنَاهُ مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا”), a direct instance of that action.
The section’s root ر ف ع is lifting from one’s resting place; here God tells Jesus “وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَيَّ,” another specific raising of a person.
This verse states of Jesus, “بَل رَّفَعَهُ اللَّهُ إِلَيْهِ,” a second Quranic formulation of the bodily raising relevant to the section’s raised-object sense.
This verse says the Mount was raised above the people (“رَفَعْنَا فَوْقَكُمُ الطُّورَ”), a concrete instance of the section’s root ر ف ع applied to a physical object.
This verse again stages the Mount raised above the people (“رَفَعْنَا فَوْقَكُمُ الطُّورَ”), repeating the physical-object sense that the section distinguishes from raised remembrance.
This verse says the Mount was raised over them (“وَرَفَعْنَا فَوْقَهُمُ الطُّورَ”), another specific physical elevation under the covenant scene.

This verse depicts the mountain lifted over the people like a canopy and feared to fall; the suspended mountain makes elevation and threatened collapse visible together, as in the section’s raised and cracking structures.
The section’s root ر ف ع includes elevation; this verse says God raises degrees whom He wills (“نَرْفَعُ دَرَجَاتٍ مَّن نَّشَاءُ”), applying the same elevation to rank rather than a building or name.
This verse says God raised some people above others in degrees (“وَرَفَعَ بَعْضَكُمْ فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ دَرَجَاتٍ”), a specific status-elevation parallel to raised remembrance.
This verse uses “نَرْفَعُ دَرَجَاتٍ مَّن نَّشَاءُ” for elevation in rank; it gives the section’s raising image a personal and social, rather than architectural, instance.
This verse describes some being raised above others in degrees (“وَرَفَعْنَا بَعْضَهُمْ فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ دَرَجَاتٍ”), a specific figurative counterpart to raised mention.

The section’s root ر ف ع reaches beyond buildings to raised remembrance; this verse says God raises believers and those given knowledge by degrees (“يَرْفَعِ اللَّهُ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا ... دَرَجَاتٍ”), another explicit elevation of standing.
The divine epithet “رَفِيعُ الدَّرَجَاتِ” names the raiser of degrees; it connects the section’s raised-height vocabulary to exalted rank in a verse about revelation.

This verse says that, had God willed, He would have raised the person by the signs (“لَرَفَعْنَاهُ بِهَا”), but he clung to earth; that stated alternative gives a specific rise/low attachment boundary to the section’s elevation motif.

The section labels root وَضْع as setting down; Mary’s “وَضَعَتْهَا” here is the distinct dictionary branch for delivering a child. The bodily release may illuminate a burden being put down, though that bridge is not explicit in the section.
